options.a: Remove excess fluid and uremic wastes and help correct electrolyte imbalances
options.b: Restore the kidney's hormone functions, such as erythropoietin and vitamin D activation
options.c: Remove protein-bound drugs and large proteins such as albumin from the blood
options.d: Lower blood pressure by delivering antihypertensive medication via dialysate

distractorExplanations.b: Dialysis does not replace endocrine kidney functions; ESAs and active vitamin D are given as separate medications.
distractorExplanations.c: The membrane is designed to retain albumin and most proteins; protein loss is a side effect, not the purpose.
distractorExplanations.d: BP improves through fluid removal; antihypertensives are not delivered through the dialysate.

options.a: Movement of water across the membrane driven by a hydrostatic pressure gradient
options.b: Movement of solutes from higher to lower concentration across a semipermeable membrane
options.c: Movement of solutes carried along with water as it crosses the membrane (solvent drag)
options.d: Binding of solutes to the membrane surface so they are removed from the blood

distractorExplanations.a: That describes ultrafiltration (fluid removal by pressure), not diffusion of solutes down a concentration gradient.
distractorExplanations.c: That is convection, the main mechanism in hemofiltration; diffusion depends on a concentration gradient.
distractorExplanations.d: That is adsorption, a minor removal mechanism for some proteins, not diffusion.

options.a: Passage of blood cells and proteins into the dialysate while retaining water and urea
options.b: Passage of water only, while all solutes including urea and potassium are retained
options.c: Passage of large proteins such as albumin while small molecules such as urea are retained
options.d: Passage of water and small/middle molecules while retaining blood cells and most proteins

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses selectivity: cells and proteins stay in the blood while water and urea cross the membrane.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes reverse osmosis behavior; urea, potassium and other small solutes must cross the dialyzer membrane.
distractorExplanations.c: Inverts size selectivity: small molecules like urea pass easily, while albumin is largely retained.

ccht-dialysis-readiness-check-dialysis-p.explanation: Membrane selectivity is fundamental; blood and dialysate remain in separate compartments. The exact molecular cutoff depends on the membrane.

options.a: Electrolyte concentration of the dialysate mixture
options.b: Bacterial and endotoxin levels in the dialysate
options.c: Temperature of the dialysate delivered to the dialyzer
options.d: Blood flow rate through the extracorporeal circuit

distractorExplanations.b: Microbial quality is measured by cultures and LAL endotoxin testing; conductivity reflects ionic concentration.
distractorExplanations.c: Temperature has its own sensor; conductivity is temperature-compensated but reflects electrolyte concentration.
distractorExplanations.d: Blood flow is set by the blood pump and seen on the pump display; conductivity is a dialysate measurement.

options.a: Fluid removal accuracy (ultrafiltration relative to dry weight)
options.b: Access recirculation (venous blood re-entering the arterial needle)
options.c: Dialysis adequacy (urea clearance relative to patient factors)
options.d: Anemia management (hemoglobin response to erythropoietin dosing)

distractorExplanations.a: UF accuracy is judged by pre/post weights against target weight; Kt/V and URR measure urea clearance.
distractorExplanations.b: Recirculation lowers adequacy but is measured with a separate recirculation study, not by Kt/V or URR.
distractorExplanations.d: Anemia is tracked with hemoglobin and iron studies; Kt/V and URR are urea-clearance adequacy measures.

options.a: Venous outflow obstruction from a kinked return line or infiltrated venous needle
options.b: A blood flow rate set too low for the size of the arterial needle in use
options.c: A dialyzer clotting downstream of the blood pump, which increases transmembrane pressure
options.d: Access inflow problems (e.g., stenosis, needle position, clotting) limiting blood flow

distractorExplanations.a: Outflow obstruction raises venous (post-dialyzer) pressure; very negative arterial pressure points to inflow.
distractorExplanations.b: A low blood flow makes arterial pressure less negative; high flow through a small needle makes it more negative.
distractorExplanations.c: Dialyzer clotting shows as rising pre-dialyzer pressure/TMP after the pump, not excessive pre-pump negativity.

options.a: Outflow obstruction such as clotting, kinked line, or infiltrated/poor venous return
options.b: Arterial needle inflow problems such as stenosis or a needle against the vessel wall
options.c: A disconnected or dislodged venous needle allowing blood to leak at the site
options.d: A blood pump speed reduced after the patient complained of cramping

distractorExplanations.b: Inflow problems drive arterial pressure more negative and can lower venous pressure rather than raise it.
distractorExplanations.c: Venous needle dislodgement drops venous pressure, which is why it may not trigger an alarm; it does not rise.
distractorExplanations.d: Lowering blood flow reduces venous pressure; a sharp rise suggests obstruction of the return path.

options.a: Detect blood leaks across the dialyzer membrane into the dialysate path
options.b: Reduce risk of air embolism by alarming and clamping if air is detected
options.c: Remove microbubbles from the dialysate before it enters the dialyzer
options.d: Monitor the arterial line for clots forming before the blood pump

distractorExplanations.a: Membrane leaks are caught by the blood leak detector on the dialysate outflow, not the venous air detector.
distractorExplanations.c: Dialysate degassing is done by the machine's deaeration system; the venous detector guards the blood path.
distractorExplanations.d: Clotting is watched through pressures and visual checks; the air detector/clamp sits on the venous return line.

options.a: Help correct metabolic alkalosis caused by uremic toxin buildup
options.b: Help remove excess calcium that accumulates in kidney failure
options.c: Help correct metabolic acidosis common in kidney failure
options.d: Help prevent clotting of the dialyzer during the treatment

distractorExplanations.a: Kidney failure causes metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis; bicarbonate is a base used to correct acidosis.
distractorExplanations.b: Calcium balance is managed with the dialysate calcium concentration; bicarbonate serves as the buffer.
distractorExplanations.d: Circuit clotting is prevented with heparin or saline flushes per order; bicarbonate has no anticoagulant role.

options.a: Pressure in the arterial line between the access and the blood pump
options.b: Pressure in the venous drip chamber reflecting resistance to blood return
options.c: Osmotic pressure difference that drives solute diffusion from blood to dialysate
options.d: Pressure gradient across the dialyzer membrane influencing ultrafiltration

distractorExplanations.a: That is arterial (pre-pump) pressure, which reflects access inflow rather than the membrane gradient.
distractorExplanations.b: That is venous pressure; TMP is the blood-to-dialysate pressure difference across the membrane.
distractorExplanations.c: Diffusion is driven by concentration gradients; TMP is a hydrostatic gradient that drives ultrafiltration.

options.a: Greater permeability allowing more middle-molecule clearance
options.b: Larger surface area allowing faster small-solute clearance like urea
options.c: Lower permeability that retains middle molecules such as beta-2 microglobulin
options.d: Greater blood flow capacity allowing pump speeds above 500 mL/min

distractorExplanations.b: Surface area and urea clearance define a high-efficiency dialyzer; flux describes membrane water permeability.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes a low-flux membrane; high-flux membranes clear more beta-2 microglobulin and other middle molecules.
distractorExplanations.d: Flux is a membrane permeability property; blood flow rate is set by the access and prescription.

ccht-dialysis-readiness-check-dialysis-p.explanation: Flux refers to water/solute permeability characteristics; prescriptions and monitoring still apply. High-flux dialyzers also require careful (volumetric) UF control.

options.a: In the same direction (cocurrent) to keep the pressure gradient stable
options.b: In opposite directions (countercurrent) to maximize diffusion gradients
options.c: In opposite directions, with dialysate flow kept below the blood flow rate
options.d: In the same direction, with dialysate recirculated to conserve concentrate

distractorExplanations.a: Cocurrent flow lets the concentration gradient fall along the fiber and lowers clearance; countercurrent is standard.
distractorExplanations.c: Dialysate flow is normally set higher than blood flow (often 500-800 mL/min) to maintain the gradient.
distractorExplanations.d: Standard in-center machines use single-pass, countercurrent dialysate; recirculating it erodes the gradient.

options.a: Start treatment with the machine in bypass and recheck conductivity after an hour
options.b: Silence the alarm and rely on the machine's internal conductivity reading alone
options.c: Not initiate or continue treatment until safe dialysate is verified; escalate per policy
options.d: Adjust the patient's prescribed sodium profile until the conductivity alarm finally clears

distractorExplanations.a: Treatment cannot start until dialysate composition is verified; bypass is a protective mode, not a workaround.
distractorExplanations.b: An out-of-range reading needs independent verification and correction, not silencing and trusting one sensor.
distractorExplanations.d: Changing the prescription masks a mixing/concentrate error and is outside the technician's scope.

options.a: How much fluid to remove (UF goal)
options.b: The dialysate sodium level to order
options.c: The blood flow rate for the session
options.d: Whether the dialyzer size is right

distractorExplanations.b: Dialysate sodium is set by the prescription and labs, not by comparing pre-weight with target weight.
distractorExplanations.c: Blood flow is set by the prescription and access performance; weight gain determines the UF goal.
distractorExplanations.d: Dialyzer choice is part of the adequacy prescription; weight versus dry weight sets fluid removal.

options.a: A dialysate temperature set cooler than the patient's body temperature
options.b: Interdialytic weight gain too small to require much fluid removal
options.c: Excessive or rapid ultrafiltration relative to vascular refill
options.d: High dialysate sodium drawing fluid out of the vascular space

distractorExplanations.a: Cool dialysate causes vasoconstriction and is used to prevent hypotension; warm dialysate contributes to it.
distractorExplanations.b: Small gains mean a low UF rate and less hypotension risk; large gains with rapid UF are the usual cause.
distractorExplanations.d: Higher dialysate sodium supports plasma osmolality and vascular refill; low sodium contributes to hypotension.

options.a: A stenosis narrowing the access that needs urgent referral
options.b: Arterial steal reducing blood flow to the hand
options.c: A clotted access that should not be cannulated
options.d: Expected blood flow through a patent access

distractorExplanations.a: A normal thrill and bruit indicate patency; stenosis shows as a high-pitched, discontinuous bruit or pulsatile thrill.
distractorExplanations.b: Steal is identified by distal hand coolness, pain or pallor, not by the presence of a thrill and bruit.
distractorExplanations.c: A clotted access has an absent thrill and bruit; their presence indicates flow through a patent access.

ccht-dialysis-readiness-check-patient-ca.explanation: Absence or marked change in thrill/bruit can signal thrombosis/stenosis—report promptly. Assess the quality of the thrill and bruit and report any change.

options.a: Adequate depth, diameter, and flow characteristics for successful cannulation
options.b: Waiting six months before the first cannulation and using 6-gauge fistula needles
options.c: Six hours of treatment per week with a minimum blood pump speed of 600 mL/min
options.d: Rotating sites six centimeters apart over six treatments per week

distractorExplanations.b: The rule uses about 6 weeks, not months; fistula needles are typically 14-17 gauge, not 6 gauge.
distractorExplanations.c: The 600 mL/min figure is access flow for maturation, not a treatment blood flow, and time is not part of it.
distractorExplanations.d: Site rotation (rope ladder) is a cannulation technique; the rule of 6s describes fistula maturation criteria.

ccht-dialysis-readiness-check-patient-ca.explanation: Maturation criteria guide when an access is ready; follow nephrology/facility standards. Classic figures: flow about 600 mL/min, diameter about 6 mm, depth under 6 mm, about 6 weeks after creation; facility protocols vary.

options.a: Arm swelling and prominent chest veins due to central vein stenosis
options.b: Hand pain, coolness, or pallor distal to the access due to ischemia
options.c: Redness, warmth, and drainage at the cannulation sites due to infection
options.d: A pulsatile, high-pitched bruit due to outflow stenosis

distractorExplanations.a: Swelling with collateral veins signals central venous stenosis/venous hypertension, not arterial steal.
distractorExplanations.c: Those are signs of access infection; steal causes ischemic symptoms distal to the access.
distractorExplanations.d: A high-pitched bruit and pulsatile access indicate outflow stenosis, not distal ischemia from steal.

options.a: Lower the blood flow rate, reposition the needle deeper into the vessel, and continue treatment
options.b: Apply heat to the site immediately and continue at the same blood flow rate
options.c: Stop the blood pump, discontinue that needle per protocol, apply pressure, and notify the nurse
options.d: Swap the arterial and venous bloodlines so blood returns through the arterial needle instead

distractorExplanations.a: Repositioning an infiltrated needle worsens the hematoma; stop the pump, remove it, hold pressure and notify.
distractorExplanations.b: Continuing flow through an infiltrated needle extends the injury; cold is usually applied first, per protocol.
distractorExplanations.d: Reversing lines does not fix an infiltrated site and increases recirculation; stop and remove the needle.

options.a: High dialysate sodium raising plasma osmolality
options.b: Hyperkalemia from a high-potassium dialysate bath
options.c: Heparin dosing that is too high for the patient
options.d: Volume/electrolyte shifts, especially aggressive UF

distractorExplanations.a: Higher sodium is used to relieve cramps; low dialysate sodium and rapid UF are associated with cramping.
distractorExplanations.b: Hyperkalemia causes weakness and arrhythmias; intradialytic cramps are linked to volume and electrolyte shifts.
distractorExplanations.c: Excess heparin causes prolonged bleeding at needle sites, not muscle cramps.

options.a: Chest pain, back pain, or anaphylactoid symptoms related to dialyzer reaction
options.b: Fever and chills appearing an hour in, from endotoxin in the water supply
options.c: Headache, nausea, and confusion from rapid urea removal in new patients
options.d: Hypotension and cramping late in treatment from excessive ultrafiltration

distractorExplanations.b: That is a pyrogenic reaction from contaminated water; first-use reactions occur within minutes of starting.
distractorExplanations.c: Those neurologic symptoms describe disequilibrium syndrome, not a dialyzer (first-use) reaction.
distractorExplanations.d: Late hypotension and cramps reflect fluid removal; first-use syndrome is an early reaction to the dialyzer.

options.a: Vital signs and post weight only, with access checked at the next session
options.b: Vital signs, access hemostasis, orthostasis, and ability to safely leave
options.c: Access hemostasis and post weight, with blood pressure taken if symptomatic
options.d: Post-treatment labs and Kt/V before the patient may leave the chair

distractorExplanations.a: Access hemostasis must be confirmed before the patient leaves; deferring it risks bleeding after discharge.
distractorExplanations.c: Post-treatment vital signs and orthostatic checks are required for every patient, not just symptomatic ones.
distractorExplanations.d: Labs are drawn on a schedule per policy; discharge criteria are vitals, hemostasis and safe ambulation.

options.a: Possible air embolism from the venous line; clamp lines and continue
options.b: Possible hyperkalemia from the dialysate bath; raise the potassium bath
options.c: Possible electrolyte imbalance such as low calcium—notify RN immediately
options.d: Possible first-use reaction to the dialyzer; slow the blood pump down

distractorExplanations.a: Air embolism presents with dyspnea, chest pain and cyanosis and requires stopping treatment, not continuing.
distractorExplanations.b: Perioral tingling with twitching suggests hypocalcemia; changing the potassium bath is outside tech scope.
distractorExplanations.d: First-use reactions occur in the first minutes with chest/back pain, not tetany-like signs near the end.

options.a: Urea is lowered too rapidly, especially in first treatments of severe uremia
options.b: Fluid is removed too rapidly in patients with large interdialytic gains
options.c: Urea is lowered too slowly in long-term patients on short treatments
options.d: Dialysate sodium is set higher than the patient's serum sodium level

distractorExplanations.b: Rapid fluid removal causes hypotension and cramps; disequilibrium comes from rapid urea (osmotic) shifts.
distractorExplanations.c: Slow urea removal means inadequate dialysis; disequilibrium results from removing urea too fast.
distractorExplanations.d: Higher dialysate sodium is a strategy to reduce disequilibrium risk, not a cause of it.

options.a: Preferred, because the wider segment is easier to hit
options.b: Avoided; cannulate healthy segments per access plan
options.c: Acceptable if a smaller 17-gauge needle is used there
options.d: Recommended as a buttonhole site to limit new punctures

distractorExplanations.a: Aneurysmal skin and wall are thin; cannulating them risks bleeding and rupture, so they are avoided.
distractorExplanations.c: Needle size does not make an aneurysm safe to puncture; the thin wall still risks rupture and bleeding.
distractorExplanations.d: Buttonhole tracks are created in healthy, straight segments, never in aneurysms.

options.a: Shorten the session as requested and document it at the end of the shift
options.b: Have the patient sign an AMA form and end treatment without involving the nurse
options.c: Inform the nurse/team, document per policy, and not coerce unsafe deviations alone
options.d: Increase the UF rate for the remaining time so the fluid goal is still met

distractorExplanations.a: A refusal must be reported to the nurse promptly so a licensed clinician can address risks and consent.
distractorExplanations.b: Informed refusal and AMA discussions are handled by licensed staff; the technician escalates first.
distractorExplanations.d: Raising UF to compensate without an order risks hypotension and is outside the technician's scope.

options.a: Patients are exposed to large volumes of water across the dialyzer membrane
options.b: Patients drink large volumes of treated water to replace removed fluid
options.c: Municipal water already meets AAMI dialysis standards once chlorine is removed
options.d: Softened water can be used directly without carbon or reverse osmosis

distractorExplanations.b: Patients are fluid-restricted; the exposure is the 100+ liters of dialysate water contacting blood per treatment.
distractorExplanations.c: Drinking-water standards are not dialysis standards; chloramine, metals, bacteria and endotoxin must be treated.
distractorExplanations.d: Softening only removes hardness; carbon and RO are still needed for chloramine and other contaminants.

options.a: Chlorine and chloramine levels
options.b: Bacteria and endotoxin counts
options.c: Calcium and magnesium (hardness)
options.d: Aluminum and other trace metals

distractorExplanations.a: Chlorine and chloramine are removed by carbon tanks; softeners exchange hardness ions.
distractorExplanations.b: Bacteria and endotoxin are controlled by RO, ultrafilters and disinfection, not by softeners.
distractorExplanations.d: Trace metals like aluminum are removed mainly by reverse osmosis; softeners target calcium and magnesium.

options.a: Removes chloramine so carbon tanks can be omitted from the system
options.b: Adds bicarbonate buffer to product water before concentrate mixing
options.c: Softens feed water by exchanging calcium for sodium ions
options.d: Removes a broad range of chemical and microbial contaminants

distractorExplanations.a: RO does not reliably remove chloramine, and chloramine damages some membranes; carbon must stay upstream.
distractorExplanations.b: RO purifies water; bicarbonate is added later from concentrate in the dialysis machine.
distractorExplanations.c: Ion exchange for hardness is the softener's job, placed upstream to protect the RO membrane.

ccht-dialysis-readiness-check-water-infe.explanation: RO is a cornerstone; reject rates, pressures, and product water quality are monitored. It does so only when functioning properly, so rejection and product water quality are monitored.

options.a: Pyrogenic reactions (fever, chills, hypotension)
options.b: Hemolysis (dark blood, chest pain, back pain)
options.c: Disequilibrium (headache, nausea, confusion)
options.d: Hypocalcemia (perioral tingling, muscle twitching)

distractorExplanations.b: Hemolysis is linked to chloramine, overheated or hypotonic dialysate, not endotoxin.
distractorExplanations.c: Disequilibrium comes from rapid urea removal; endotoxin causes pyrogenic reactions.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypocalcemia relates to dialysate calcium/electrolyte shifts, not endotoxin exposure.

options.a: Remove chloramine that passes through the carbon tanks into the loop
options.b: Control bacterial biofilm and keep microbial counts within standards
options.c: Restore RO membrane rejection after scale buildup from hard water
options.d: Sterilize the distribution loop so water cultures are no longer needed

distractorExplanations.a: Chloramine breakthrough is handled by carbon tank testing and replacement; disinfection targets microbes.
distractorExplanations.c: Scale is handled by softening and membrane cleaning; disinfection controls biofilm and bacteria.
distractorExplanations.d: Disinfection controls biofilm but does not sterilize; routine cultures and endotoxin tests are still required.

options.a: Isolating HBsAg+ patients in a negative-pressure room, as is done for airborne spread
options.b: Reusing dialyzers for HBsAg+ patients only after an extra bleach disinfection step
options.c: Vaccination, screening, dedicated equipment/separation practices for HBsAg+ patients
options.d: Monthly HBsAg testing of immune patients with treatment at any station

distractorExplanations.a: HBV is bloodborne; CDC calls for a dedicated room/area, machine and staff, not airborne isolation.
distractorExplanations.b: CDC advises that HBsAg+ patients not participate in dialyzer reuse programs at all.
distractorExplanations.d: Immune (anti-HBs positive) patients are tested annually; HBsAg+ patients need a dedicated station.

ccht-dialysis-readiness-check-water-infe.explanation: Dialysis populations have historically elevated HBV risk; infection control is specialized and strict. These practices follow CDC recommendations for dialysis units.

options.a: Before gloving at the start of each shift, with glove changes replacing it between each patient
options.b: After patient contact and blood exposure, but skipped before contact when wearing gloves
options.c: Before each cannulation and after each disconnection, with alcohol pads in between
options.d: Before and after patient contact and after contact with blood, fluids, or contaminated surfaces

distractorExplanations.a: Glove changes do not replace hand hygiene; it is needed before and after each patient contact.
distractorExplanations.b: Hand hygiene is required before donning gloves for patient contact, not only afterward.
distractorExplanations.c: Limits hygiene to two procedures; it is required at every patient/station contact and after contamination.

options.a: Promptly with EPA-registered disinfectant appropriate for bloodborne pathogens, using PPE
options.b: Promptly with soap and water, then left to air dry before the next patient sits
options.c: At the end of the shift with full-strength bleach, since cleaning it earlier only spreads it
options.d: Promptly by spraying disinfectant directly onto the blood without wiping it up first

distractorExplanations.b: Soap and water removes soil but does not disinfect; an EPA-registered disinfectant is required.
distractorExplanations.c: Blood spills are cleaned immediately; waiting exposes patients and staff to bloodborne pathogens.
distractorExplanations.d: Visible blood must be absorbed and removed first; organic material blocks the disinfectant.

ccht-dialysis-readiness-check-water-infe.explanation: Immediate spill response protects patients and staff. Follow facility policy for the product and contact time.

options.a: Repeat the culture next month and act if the limit is exceeded a second time
options.b: Investigation, disinfection/corrective action, and possible treatment adjustments
options.c: Documentation only, since action levels are set above the maximum allowable limit
options.d: Replacing the RO membrane before any investigation of the source of contamination

distractorExplanations.a: Exceeding the action level requires prompt corrective action, not waiting for a second failed culture.
distractorExplanations.c: Action levels are set below the maximum allowable limit so problems are corrected before limits are breached.
distractorExplanations.d: The source must be investigated first; contamination often comes from loop biofilm, not the membrane.

ccht-dialysis-readiness-check-water-infe.explanation: Quality results drive corrective actions; technicians escalate abnormal findings. Actions are directed by the medical director and facility policy.

options.a: Change gloves between patients but keep the same pair for clean and dirty tasks at one station
options.b: Return unused supplies from a patient station to the clean cart if the packaging looks intact
options.c: Avoid carrying contaminated items to clean areas and change gloves/hygiene between dirty and clean tasks
options.d: Carry medication vials and supplies in pockets between stations to cut down on trips back to the clean area

distractorExplanations.a: Gloves must also be changed when moving from dirty to clean tasks at the same station.
distractorExplanations.b: CDC advises items taken to a station not be returned to common clean areas, even if unopened.
distractorExplanations.d: Pockets carry contamination between stations; supplies should come from the clean area as needed.

options.a: Treat all blood and certain body fluids as potentially infectious
options.b: Treat blood as infectious only for patients with a known positive test
options.c: Use airborne precautions for every patient during dialysis treatment
options.d: Use PPE for cannulation, with gloves optional for routine machine checks

distractorExplanations.b: Standard precautions apply to every patient because infection status is often unknown.
distractorExplanations.c: Airborne precautions are transmission-based for specific infections; standard precautions cover blood and fluids.
distractorExplanations.d: Machine surfaces and lines can be blood-contaminated; gloves are needed whenever exposure is possible.

options.a: Kept at the patient station and shared between neighboring patients' doses
options.b: Handled with aseptic technique; ideally dedicated per patient
options.c: Entered with a new needle but the same syringe for consecutive patients
options.d: Wiped with alcohol once daily, after which the septum can be punctured freely

distractorExplanations.a: CDC: medications are prepared in a clean area away from stations; shared vials at stations spread HBV/HCV.
distractorExplanations.c: A new needle on a used syringe still contaminates the vial; needle and syringe must both be new.
distractorExplanations.d: The septum is disinfected with alcohol before every entry, not once a day.

ccht-dialysis-readiness-check-water-infe.explanation: CDC outbreak lessons emphasize medication preparation safety in dialysis units. Dedicated single-patient use is required when policy or outbreak guidance calls for it.

options.a: Remove chloramine that passes through the carbon tanks
options.b: Remove excess sodium so conductivity stays within range
options.c: Further reduce bacteria/endotoxin in dialysate delivery
options.d: Remove air bubbles from dialysate before the dialyzer

distractorExplanations.a: Chloramine is removed by carbon tanks upstream; ultrafilters remove bacteria and endotoxin.
distractorExplanations.b: Sodium and conductivity depend on concentrate proportioning; ultrafilters do not adjust electrolytes.
distractorExplanations.d: Air is removed by the machine's deaeration system; ultrafilters provide extra microbial filtration.

options.a: Alarms, conductivity/temperature in range, and extracorporeal circuit integrity
options.b: Conductivity and temperature only, since alarm tests run during treatment
options.c: Alarm tests and patient weight, with conductivity checked after cannulation
options.d: Dialyzer size and heparin dose, with alarm tests done weekly by biomed staff

distractorExplanations.b: Alarm tests are part of the pre-treatment checks and must pass before the patient is connected.
distractorExplanations.c: Conductivity must be verified before treatment starts, not after the patient is cannulated.
distractorExplanations.d: Alarm testing is done before every treatment by the operator; biomed handles scheduled maintenance.

ccht-dialysis-readiness-check-safety-doc.explanation: Pre-treatment checks prevent many adverse events. Follow the facility checklist each time.

options.a: Pre and post vital signs and weights, with machine settings recorded only when an alarm has occurred
options.b: Vital signs, machine parameters, UF/goal, access, medications given per role, and significant events
options.c: Machine parameters and UF totals, with access condition charted by the nurse once weekly
options.d: Vital signs every two hours and significant events, with medications charted by pharmacy

distractorExplanations.a: Machine parameters are recorded routinely during treatment, not only when alarms occur.
distractorExplanations.c: Access condition is assessed and documented every treatment, not weekly.
distractorExplanations.d: Vitals are typically recorded at least every 30 minutes, and medications are charted by whoever gives them.

options.a: By the end of the shift, after the treatment schedule is completed
options.b: Within 7 days, once the source patient's test results are available
options.c: Immediately per exposure control plan, with first aid and evaluation
options.d: Immediately, but only if the source patient is known to be HBV positive

distractorExplanations.a: Post-exposure prophylaxis is time-sensitive; reporting is immediate under the exposure control plan.
distractorExplanations.b: Reporting cannot wait for source results; evaluation and prophylaxis decisions start right away.
distractorExplanations.d: Every needlestick is reported regardless of known source status; HCV/HIV risk also applies.

options.a: Respond promptly, ensure patient safety, troubleshoot per training, and escalate if unresolved
options.b: Reset the alarm first, then check the patient and machine if it sounds again within minutes
options.c: Widen the alarm limits so the treatment can continue and recheck at the next vital signs
options.d: Call biomedical staff first and wait for them before checking the patient or the lines

distractorExplanations.b: Resetting before assessing ignores the cause; check the patient and circuit before clearing the alarm.
distractorExplanations.c: Widening limits to stop alarms defeats the safety system and can hide a dangerous condition.
distractorExplanations.d: The technician assesses the patient and circuit immediately; biomed is called for unresolved machine faults.

options.a: Annual state survey preparation focused on correcting deficiencies cited
options.b: Ongoing quality assessment and performance improvement for outcomes and safety
options.c: Individual staff performance reviews and disciplinary tracking for errors
options.d: Quarterly infection audits conducted by an outside accrediting agency

distractorExplanations.a: Survey readiness is a result of QAPI, but QAPI is a continuous program, not annual survey prep.
distractorExplanations.c: QAPI is a system-level improvement program; staff evaluations are a separate HR process.
distractorExplanations.d: QAPI is run internally by the interdisciplinary team, not by an outside agency's audits.

options.a: Discuss patient information freely within the clinic, including with other patients
options.b: Share patient details with family members who call, as long as they know the birth date
options.c: Discuss patient information only with those involved in care and per privacy rules
options.d: Discuss cases in hallways or the break room if the patient's full name is not used

distractorExplanations.a: HIPAA limits PHI to those involved in care; other patients and uninvolved staff have no right to it.
distractorExplanations.b: Knowing a birth date is not authorization; disclosure to family requires patient permission per policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Other identifiers still reveal identity, and conversations outside care needs violate minimum-necessary use.

options.a: Propping fire doors open during treatment so patients can be evacuated faster
options.b: Using extension cords and power strips for machines when outlets are limited
options.c: Evacuating all patients first, before disconnecting them from their dialysis machines
options.d: Keeping exits clear, knowing extinguisher locations, and not using damaged cords

distractorExplanations.a: Fire doors must stay closed or on approved release devices to contain smoke and fire.
distractorExplanations.b: Extension cords and power strips for medical equipment are a fire and electrical hazard and not permitted.
distractorExplanations.c: Patients must be clamped and disconnected (emergency takeoff) before they can be evacuated.

options.a: Adjust dry weight and UF goals independently once they hold national certification
options.b: Perform delegated technical tasks and escalate clinical decisions to licensed nurses/providers
options.c: Administer any IV medication on the order sheet, including drugs restricted to licensed nurses
options.d: Assess patients and change the dialysis prescription whenever the nurse is unavailable

distractorExplanations.a: Certification does not expand scope; dry weight and UF goal changes need an order or RN involvement.
distractorExplanations.c: Medication administration is limited by state law and policy; restricted drugs stay with licensed nurses.
distractorExplanations.d: Assessment and prescription changes are licensed functions; the technician escalates instead.

ccht-dialysis-readiness-check-safety-doc.explanation: Technicians are vital but practice within defined limits. Delegation follows state law and facility policy.

options.a: Staff need the manufacturer's operating instructions for a dialysis machine
options.b: Staff need the patient's allergy and medication history before treatment
options.c: Staff need hazard and first-aid information about chemicals used in the facility
options.d: Staff need results of monthly water cultures and endotoxin testing

distractorExplanations.a: Operating instructions come from the operator's manual; SDSs cover chemical hazards and first aid.
distractorExplanations.b: Allergy and medication history is in the medical record, not on a chemical Safety Data Sheet.
distractorExplanations.d: Water culture results are in the water quality logs; SDSs describe chemical hazards.

options.a: Allows the monthly water culture to be skipped when the cycles have been recorded
options.b: Records the conductivity and pH readings taken before each treatment
options.c: Shows the machine's preventive maintenance and alarm calibration status
options.d: Provides evidence that required cleaning/disinfection cycles were completed

distractorExplanations.a: Disinfection logs do not replace microbial cultures; both are required.
distractorExplanations.b: Pre-treatment conductivity and pH are recorded on the treatment flowsheet, not the disinfection log.
distractorExplanations.c: Preventive maintenance and calibration are tracked in biomedical service records, not disinfection logs.

options.a: Ask the nurse/supervisor and follow policy rather than guessing
options.b: Perform it if a coworker with more experience says it is allowed
options.c: Perform it if the patient consents and it was covered in training
options.d: Check online forums for what other technicians do in that case

distractorExplanations.b: Peer opinion does not define scope; the nurse/supervisor and written policy do.
distractorExplanations.c: Patient consent and training do not authorize a task outside the technician's defined role.
distractorExplanations.d: Practices vary by state and facility; online forums are not an authority on your scope.

options.a: Replace the nurse in leading codes when a technician is present
options.b: Respond rapidly to respiratory/cardiac emergencies in the unit
options.c: Use the AED only after the physician arrives at the bedside
options.d: Pass the annual survey checklist of required emergency items

distractorExplanations.a: Technicians assist in emergencies per role; leading resuscitation stays with licensed staff.
distractorExplanations.c: AEDs are designed for immediate use by trained staff; waiting for a physician delays defibrillation.
distractorExplanations.d: Survey compliance is secondary; the purpose of readiness is a rapid response to real emergencies.

options.a: Weighing pre-treatment and estimating the post weight from the UF total removed
options.b: Using whichever scale is free and averaging the two values when the readings conflict
options.c: Same scale conditions when possible, shoes/outerwear consistency, and documented values
options.d: Weighing with the patient's coat and shoes on pre and off post for comfort

distractorExplanations.a: Post weight must be measured; estimating from UF totals hides machine or fluid-intake discrepancies.
distractorExplanations.b: Scales should be consistent, and conflicting values need investigation rather than averaging.
distractorExplanations.d: Inconsistent clothing between weights creates false fluid-removal figures and UF errors.
